title: Cross-border fast payments grew through regional networks with different designs
summary: Cam Donohoe, Oliver Junye Xu and Youming Liu compile 62 operational arrangements connecting payment systems across 124 jurisdictions. Their 286 observations span arrangements launched from November 1975 to June 2026. The long history reveals a change in what gets connected. Until the early 2010s, new links appeared gradually and almost entirely between wholesale systems. Subsequent growth has come predominantly from fast retail payment systems, especially QR-code arrangements in Asia. The resulting networks remain largely regional. Differences in their design determine what two countries being “linked” actually means for the infrastructure that carries a payment (dataset overview and figures 2–6).

The dataset records public sector-facilitated links across existing payment systems. It includes both large-value wholesale infrastructure and retail systems used for smaller payments. Each row pairs an arrangement with a participating jurisdiction. Thailand and Singapore therefore account for two observations in their bilateral PromptPay–PayNow link. A common platform spanning many countries produces one row for each participant. Counting rows as separate payment corridors would overstate how many independent arrangements exist. The appendix distinguishes the date an arrangement launched from the date an individual jurisdiction joined. They can be years apart for a multilateral system that expanded over time (table A1 and dataset overview).

The taxonomy also separates the way payment instructions travel from the way money settles. A cross-border QR code can give a customer a common way to initiate a merchant payment, even if correspondent banks or an existing infrastructure link still settle the transaction. The authors include these as a lighter form of bilateral arrangement because participating jurisdictions establish contractual and operational links. An intermediary hub can instead account for and clear payments between multiple systems. A shared platform can let payment service providers in different jurisdictions reach one another through the same infrastructure. A count of links alone cannot establish how many intermediaries a transaction traverses, the currencies it can use or the price a customer pays (background and figure A1).

This distinction helps explain the map. Europe, Africa and the Middle East predominantly use shared platforms in the fast-payment networks examined. India’s Unified Payments Interface forms the centre of a set of bilateral connections. Southeast Asia has developed a web of bilateral links without a single central node. Of 33 Asian fast-payment arrangements in the dataset, 28 are QR links. Figure 5 draws connections among jurisdictions participating in the same arrangement, so a line on that map need not denote an independent bilateral corridor. Figure 6 separately identifies full fast-payment and QR links in Southeast Asia. Table 2 keeps announced but unlaunched arrangements outside the operational totals.

For anyone assessing opportunities in cross-border payments, these data describe which infrastructure exists and how jurisdictions participate. They supply no transaction volumes, revenue shares or measures of end-user savings. The collection covers arrangements still operating, and the authors flag inconsistent documentation. Launch dates are generally more reliable than dates of entry by individual jurisdictions, especially for older multilateral systems. Evidence is more readily available for Europe and parts of Asia-Pacific than for several other regions, where secondary material was sometimes necessary. The apparent distribution of activity should therefore be read alongside the coverage and classification rules in the appendix, particularly before comparing rates of adoption across regions.

questions.question: Do full fast-payment links produce different customer outcomes from QR arrangements?
questions.detail: The dataset identifies launch, geography and design but lacks standardized information about prices, speed, settlement certainty or transaction volumes. Match comparable corridors to retail payment data before and after launch, separating person-to-person transfers from merchant payments. That would test whether a technical distinction in the classification predicts a measurable improvement for the particular customers an arrangement serves.

questions.question: What accounts for the choice between a common platform, a central hub and bilateral links?
questions.detail: The maps describe substantial regional differences without measuring which design is more resilient or cheaper to expand. Compare implementation costs, governance and the time needed for an additional jurisdiction to join. Distinguish a single multilateral launch from several bilateral agreements, and check results against the appendix’s warnings about the precision of historical entry dates.

questions.question: How much would incomplete historical coverage change the shift from wholesale to retail?
questions.detail: The authors identify currently operating arrangements and report uneven source quality across regions and periods. Older discontinued links or poorly documented launches could change the denominator used for historical comparisons. Build a supplementary inventory from dated operator and central bank records, identify closures and flag uncertain start dates. Recalculate the wholesale and retail series with explicit ranges for missing observations.
